interactions.label: During a cardiovascular examination of a 3-year-old who is calm on the parent's

params.question: During a cardiovascular examination of a 3-year-old who is calm on the parent's lap but becomes distressed when laid supine, what is the most appropriate approach?

answers.text: Insist on the strict IPPA order, beginning with inspection in the supine position

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rigid adherence to textbook order means auscultation will be unreliable once the child becomes distressed. The opportunistic approach is standard in paediatric practice.

answers.text: Defer the cardiac examination entirely until the child can be sedated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sedation is unnecessary and disproportionate. Adapting the examination sequence to the child's temperament is the standard clinical approach.

answers.text: Auscultate the heart while the child is calm on the parent's lap, completing the remaining steps afterward

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — a skilled examiner auscultates when the child is quiet, even if this departs from the textbook IPPA order. A crying child cannot be reliably auscultated, so this opportunity must not be missed.

answers.text: Rely solely on peripheral pulse palpation without attempting cardiac auscultation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Peripheral pulses are important but cannot substitute for cardiac auscultation when evaluating murmurs, heart sounds, and rhythm.

overallFeedback.feedback: In paediatric CVS examination, auscultation when the child is calm takes priority over rigid textbook order. The full structured IPPA sequence is completed afterward.
Correct! Clinical flexibility is key — auscultate while the child is calm, then complete the remaining IPPA steps systematically.

interactions.label: Which symptom cluster is shared by left-to-right shunt lesions such as VSD, ASD,

params.question: Which symptom cluster is shared by left-to-right shunt lesions such as VSD, ASD, and PDA?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These features characterise cyanotic heart disease with right-to-left shunting, not acyanotic left-to-right shunts.

answers.text: Exertional syncope, chest pain, and diminished peripheral pulses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These features suggest obstructive lesions such as aortic stenosis or coarctation of the aorta, not left-to-right shunt lesions.

answers.text: Failure to thrive, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and cardiac failure in infancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — left-to-right shunts cause pulmonary overcirculation and volume overload, leading to failure to thrive, recurrent LRTIs from pulmonary congestion, and cardiac failure from sustained volume overload.
This combination describes acute rheumatic fever (Jones Criteria), not congenital heart disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, PDA) all cause pulmonary overcirculation — the shared consequences are failure to thrive, recurrent lower respiratory infections, and cardiac failure in infancy.
Correct! Pulmonary overcirculation from left-to-right shunts produces the characteristic triad of failure to thrive, recurrent LRTIs, and cardiac failure.

interactions.label: Ankle oedema and orthopnoea are the most common presenting features of cardiac f

params.question: Ankle oedema and orthopnoea are the most common presenting features of cardiac failure in infants.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect — ankle oedema and orthopnoea are rarely seen in infants with cardiac failure. The most common presentation is feeding difficulty and failure to thrive, which distinguishes cardiac failure from simple respiratory infection in this age group.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the 'classic' adult features of ankle oedema and orthopnoea are rarely seen in infants. Cardiac failure in infants presents predominantly with feeding difficulty and failure to thrive, resulting from the increased metabolic demand and work of breathing during feeds.

params.question: Which feature best distinguishes subacute infective endocarditis (Streptococcus viridans) from acute infective endocarditis (Staphylococcus aureus) in children?

answers.text: Subacute IE causes high-spiking fever with rigors, whereas acute IE manifests as persistent low-grade fever over weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is reversed. Subacute IE from Streptococcus viridans causes low-grade, persistent fever over weeks, while acute Staphylococcal IE produces high fever with systemic toxicity.

answers.text: Both forms are caused by Gram-negative organisms, but subacute IE responds better to oral antibiotics than acute IE

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both are caused by Gram-positive organisms — Streptococcus viridans and Staphylococcus aureus are both Gram-positive cocci. Neither form is treated with oral antibiotics alone.

answers.text: Subacute IE presents as a smouldering, weeks-long febrile illness with gradual peripheral stigmata; acute IE produces a rapid, toxic presentation within days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — the tempo of illness is the key distinguishing feature. Streptococcus viridans causes an insidious illness with gradual development of peripheral manifestations, while Staphylococcus aureus produces fulminant sepsis with rapid valve destruction.

answers.text: Subacute IE spares the heart valves entirely, while acute IE causes rapid destruction limited to the mitral valve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both forms damage heart valves. Valve destruction is actually more rapid and severe in acute Staphylococcal IE, and it is not limited to the mitral valve alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction is the tempo of illness: subacute IE (Strep viridans) smoulders over weeks with gradual peripheral stigmata, while acute IE (Staph aureus) is rapid, toxic, and life-threatening within days.
Correct! The tempo — smouldering versus fulminant — is the cardinal clinical distinction between subacute and acute infective endocarditis.
